title: Standard enthalpies of formation and combustion; Hess's law cycles; Bond enthalpies
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EN03#t3 term and clue written for the game; EN04#t1 term and clue written for the game; EN05#t3 term and clue written for the game; EN04#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN03#N.10a, EN04#N.9a, EN05#N.6, EN04#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Exothermic
items.clue: Describes the forming of a bond: energy is released.

items.label: Hess's law
items.clue: States that the total ΔH for a change is the same whichever route is taken.

items.label: Enthalpy of combustion
items.clue: ΔH for complete burning, with carbon ending as CO₂(g) and hydrogen as H₂O(l).

items.label: Conservation of energy
items.clue: The principle that no route from reactants to products can create or destroy it.

questions.stem: CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g), ΔH = −99 kJ mol⁻¹. Bond enthalpies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432. What value for the C–Cl bond enthalpy do these data give?
questions.explanation: One C–H and one Cl–Cl break (656 kJ); one C–Cl and one H–Cl form. 656 − (x + 432) = −99, so x = 323 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Use the enthalpy changes of reactions 1 and 2 to calculate ΔH for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Reaction 1: H₂(g) + O₂(g) → H₂O₂(l), ΔH₁ = −187.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Reaction 2: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH₂ = −571.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Reverse and double reaction 1: +375.6. Add reaction 2: −571.6. 2H₂ and one O₂ cancel. ΔH = −196.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol?
questions.explanation: 1 mol of ethanol burns completely to CO₂(g) and H₂O(l). Check: 7 O atoms on each side.

questions.stem: Graphite turns into diamond only at enormous pressures, so ΔH for C(s, graphite) → C(s, diamond) can't be measured directly. But both forms burn. (1) C(s, graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ · (2) C(s, diamond) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −395.4 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for graphite → diamond?
questions.explanation: Keep (1); reverse (2), so its ΔH becomes +395.4. Add: CO₂ and O₂ cancel. ΔH = −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
